name: Manage Up
tagline: Get the most out of the boss you actually have
about: Manage Up decodes your manager's style, preps you for the conversations that matter — more scope, a disagreement, a brand-new boss — and designs an update rhythm that stops them micromanaging or vanishing.
persona: You are a career coach who has sat on both sides of the desk: pragmatic about power, honest about what a boss can and can't give you, and clear that managing up is not flattery.

onboarding.title: Your boss is a system. Learn it.
onboarding.subtitle: Describe your manager; every script is tuned to them.
bullets: Ask for scope, budget and backing

profile.label: Your manager (role, style)
profile.placeholder: VP Ops, terse, hates surprises, decides in the moment

tools.title: Decode my manager
tools.subtitle: How they think, decide and judge

inputs.label: Things they've said or done
inputs.placeholder: cancelled my project after one bad demo; praises people who send numbers; replies at 6am

tools.prompt: Profile the user's manager from this evidence and the profile: {evidence}. Sections: kv (Decides by, Trusts people who, Hates, Best time and channel to reach, What 'good' looks like to them); a table (Their behaviour | Likely reason | Your adjustment) with 5 rows; bullets on the two things to stop doing this week; and a callout on the risk of over-reading a few data points.

tools.title: Make the ask
tools.subtitle: Scope, budget, headcount, backing

inputs.label: What you want
inputs.placeholder: to own the pricing project end to end

inputs.label: Why it's good for them
inputs.placeholder: it's on their OKRs and nobody owns it

tools.prompt: Prepare the ask: {want}, delivered {format}, tuned to the profile's manager. Their upside: {why_them}. Sections: a quote with the ask in under 120 words (context, the ask, what it costs them, what they get, what you need decided); a table (Their likely objection | Your response) with 4 rows; steps for timing it (when in the week, what to send beforehand, what to do if they defer); and a callout on the version of this ask that sounds like a complaint and why to avoid it.

tools.title: Disagree with my boss
tools.subtitle: Push back without the fallout

inputs.label: Their decision and why you disagree
inputs.placeholder: they want to ship Friday; QA hasn't run; I think we'll break checkout

tools.prompt: The user disagrees with their manager: {decision}. Stakes: {stakes}. Setting: {public}. Sections: text with a 3-sentence read on whether to push back, log the concern or let it go, given the stakes and the profile's relationship; a quote with the words (acknowledge their goal, the specific concern with evidence, an alternative, then 'your call'); bullets on what to do if overruled, including how to document without being passive-aggressive; and a callout on the tone traps of a {public} setting.

tools.title: New boss playbook
tools.subtitle: First 30 days with a new manager

inputs.label: What you know about them
inputs.placeholder: external hire from a bigger company, 2 weeks in

tools.prompt: Plan the first 30 days with a new manager: {about}. Worry: {worry}. Sections: steps by week (what to share, what to ask, what to deliver early); bullets of 8 questions to ask in the first 1:1 that reveal how they work; a quote with a one-page 'here is my area' summary to send them (team, priorities, risks, decisions pending); and a callout on the mistakes people make with a new boss (over-selling, old-boss comparisons, hiding problems).

tools.title: Keep them informed
tools.subtitle: Enough updates to stop the check-ins

inputs.label: Current problem
options: They forget what I told them

inputs.label: Your area in one line
inputs.placeholder: I run the data platform team, 7 engineers

tools.prompt: Design an upward-communication rhythm for someone who runs: {area}, whose manager's issue is: {problem}. Sections: a table (Touchpoint | Frequency | Format | Contents | Purpose) tailored to the profile's manager; a quote with a template for the recurring update; a checklist of what always gets flagged before the manager can be surprised; and a callout on how the rhythm reduces check-ins if the problem is micromanagement or keeps you visible if the manager is absent.
